strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and challenging problem: text-guided color editing with preservation of geometry, material properties, illumination, and non-edited regions. The proposed ColorCtrl is training-free and targets modern MM-DiT backbones such as SD3 and FLUX.1-dev.

The method gives a clear MM-DiT-specific attention decomposition and uses it in a unified pipeline: vision-to-vision transfer for structure preservation, vision-to-text-based masking plus value-token copying for color preservation, and text-to-vision attention scaling for attribute re-weighting.

The approach is model-agnostic and is demonstrated on image models (SD3, FLUX.1-dev), a video model (CogVideoX), and instruction-based editing models (Step1X-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext dev), which strengthens the generality claim.

The empirical study is extensive: PIE-Bench and ColorCtrl-Bench, multiple training-free and commercial baselines, ablations, additional structural and perceptual metrics, user study, real-image editing, multi-object editing, and limitations. Quantitative consistency metrics generally favor the proposed method.

The paper provides useful practical insights, especially the observation that text-to-vision attention is better for mask localization than text-to-vision/text-to-vision averages, and that scaling before softmax is preferable to post-softmax re-weighting.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core operations are adaptations of existing attention-control editing ideas (e.g., Prompt-to-Prompt, MasaCtrl, DiTCtrl) to MM-DiT, with incremental changes such as copying vision-to-vision attention maps and non-edited value tokens. The rendering-process formulation is conceptual and is not actually used by the method to infer or enforce physical parameters.

The commercial-model comparison is not fully fair: the main benchmark results for the proposed method are obtained in a noise-to-image setting with fixed seeds, while FLUX.1 Kontext Max and GPT-4o are evaluated on PIE-Bench source images in a real-image editing setting. This weakens the central claim that ColorCtrl surpasses commercial models in consistency, even though real-image results are reported separately in the appendix without the same commercial comparison.

The method relies on benchmark-provided target words such as PIE-Bench's 'blended_word' for mask extraction and attribute selection. This means the editing pipeline is not fully automatic from a free-form text prompt, and the claim of requiring no manual tuning overlooks this dependence.

Claims about editing light-source color and ambient illumination are not quantitatively validated: the main benchmark focuses on object albedo/color changes, and it is unclear how the mask-based color preservation localizes and preserves non-object global illumination effects.
Video evaluation lacks an explicit temporal-consistency metric; the temporal-coherence claim is supported mainly by frame-wise averaged metrics and qualitative examples.

The user study is small and the table reports 0 preference for all training-free baselines, which is surprisingly strong and would benefit from more explanation, per-case breakdowns, and statistical reporting.

Although additional SC/PQ metrics mitigate CLIP's limitations, the proposed method still trails commercial baselines on semantic edit success (SC), so the claim of state-of-the-art 'edit quality' needs more nuance.

strengths: Addresses a practical and visually important problem: text-guided color editing in images and videos with training-free MM-DiT attention control.

The overall pipeline is clearly motivated: structure preservation via vision-to-vision attention transfer, color preservation via non-edit region value-token copying, and optional attribute re-weighting.
Provides extensive experiments across multiple backbones (SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, Step1X-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext dev) and several training-free/commercial baselines.
Reports strong consistency metrics (Canny-SSIM, background PSNR/SSIM) and includes additional structural/editing metrics in the appendix.
Includes ablation studies, real-image editing examples, user study, and a promised code release with implementation details.
Qualitative results demonstrate visually coherent color changes and preservation of some material/reflection effects in several examples.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method combines existing attention-control editing ideas (self-attention map transfer, attention-based mask extraction, value-token copying, attention re-weighting) adapted to MM-DiT, with little new theoretical or algorithmic insight.

The central claim of physical consistency is not adequately supported: the method does not explicitly infer or enforce rendering parameters (geometry, material, illumination), and the evaluation does not measure albedo vs. light-source separation, light-matter interaction, or material consistency in a quantitative way.

Evaluation protocol is questionable: the main benchmark uses a noise-to-image setting rather than real-image editing, making the task easier and less realistic; real-image editing is relegated to the appendix and limited comparisons.
Benchmark scale and validity: main PIE-Bench evaluation uses only 40 prompt pairs, and the proposed ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by GPT and not independently validated for quality or diversity.

Quantitative evidence is mixed: CLIP similarity is often lower than baselines or commercial models, yet the paper dismisses CLIP as over-saturated; the stronger VIEScore metrics appear only in the appendix, and SC scores are lower than commercial models.

Baseline fairness is uncertain: several baselines are reimplemented and hyperparameter-tuned by the authors, and some were not originally designed for MM-DiT or color editing; stronger instruction-based editing baselines are not compared in the main experiments.

The attribute re-weighting contribution is only qualitatively demonstrated; there is no quantitative evaluation of control fidelity, no baseline comparison, and limited evidence for word-level intensity control.
Generalization to video and instruction-based editing models is primarily qualitative and narrow (e.g., only CogVideoX-2B for video), so the claimed broad applicability is not fully established.
User study is limited and suspiciously extreme: 24 participants over 34 cases, with all training-free baselines receiving 0 preference, which requires more careful reporting and statistical analysis.
Reproducibility is incomplete: code is not yet available, and the sensitivity of results to baseline hyperparameters and mask thresholds is not fully explored.

Overbroad claims: terms such as “film industry-level,” “physically consistent,” and “surpasses commercial models” are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given different training data and interfaces for commercial baselines.
Clarity/positioning issues: the rendering formulation is not meaningfully integrated into the method, the main paper is dense, and several important results are placed in the appendix.

strengths: Presents a training-free color editing method for MM-DiT models that edits albedo, light source color, and ambient lighting while aiming to preserve geometry, material, and light-matter interaction consistency.

Introduces a clear attention-control strategy exploiting the joint text-vision attention of MM-DiT: structure preservation via vision-to-vision attention transfer, color preservation via a mask extracted from vision-to-text attention and value-token copying, and word-level attribute re-weighting before softmax.
Avoids manual selection of attention layers and timesteps, making the method more robust and easier to apply across backbones than prior attention-control editing methods such as DiTCtrl.

Extensive evaluation across SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX-2B, and instruction-based editing models, with both training-free and commercial baselines, a new ColorCtrl-Bench, user studies, ablations, and additional structural/editing-quality metrics.
Quantitative results show strong consistency preservation, especially in Canny SSIM and background PSNR/SSIM, and the video extension demonstrates improved temporal coherence.
Qualitative examples show natural handling of reflections, shadows, material properties, multi-object edits, and word-level attribute intensity control.
Clear and relevant positioning within text-guided editing and MM-DiT literature, with useful discussion of the functional roles of the four attention quadrants.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the overall attention-control editing paradigm is established, and components such as attention-map transfer, mask-based latent preservation, and value-token copying have close analogues in prior work.

Several implementation details are not fully specified, including how mask extraction is aggregated across layers and timesteps, the exact stage at which attention maps are manipulated relative to softmax, how source and target token sequences are aligned for different prompts, and the re-weighting scale factors.

The claim of preserving physical consistency and light-matter interactions is supported mainly visually and conceptually; the rendering formulation is not actually enforced or quantitatively evaluated for reflection, refraction, or illumination consistency.

The main benchmark uses a noise-to-image setting rather than real-image inversion, so the method's robustness to real-image inversion is only evaluated in the appendix; the new ColorCtrl-Bench is also generated by an LLM and only partially human-reviewed.

CLIP similarity is lower than commercial baselines, and while the authors argue that CLIP favors over-saturated edits, this argument is not fully definitive without stronger physical or human judgement metrics.
Attribute re-weighting is demonstrated qualitatively but lacks quantitative evaluation of monotonicity, controllability, or user preference.
The user study is relatively small (24 participants, 34 cases), and the reported 0% preference for all training-free baselines raises questions about statistical reliability and presentation design.

Some claims are overstated, such as "film industry-level" color changing and general "state-of-the-art" performance, since the commercial comparison is based primarily on consistency rather than overall edit quality.
